rows.ask: Who created Rust and in what year did it first appear?

core: Graydon Hoare created Rust in 2006 while working at Mozilla.
Rust first appeared on January 19, 2012.
adjacent: Hoare started the Rust project as a personal project due to frustration with a broken elevator in his apartment building whose software had crashed.
Rust was named after the group of fungi of the same name that is 'over-engineered for survival'.
Between 2006 and 2009, Rust was not publicized to others at Mozilla and was written in Hoare's free time.
Mozilla officially sponsored the Rust project in 2009.
Hoare began speaking about the language around 2009 after a small group at Mozilla became interested in the project.
During the early years, the Rust compiler was written in about 38,000 lines of OCaml.
Brendan Eich and other Mozilla executives placed engineers on the project including Patrick Walton, Niko Matsakis, Felix Klock, and Manish Goregaokar.
The ownership system was in place by 2010.
The Rust logo was developed in 2011 based on a bicycle chainring.
Rust 0.1 became the first public release on January 20, 2012 for Windows, Linux, and MacOS.
Graydon Hoare stepped down from Rust in 2013.
After Hoare's departure, Rust evolved under a federated governance structure with a 'core team' of initially six people.
Rust 1.0 was published on May 15, 2015, becoming the first stable release.
Hoare cited languages from the 1970s, 1980s, and 1990s as influences including CLU, BETA, Mesa, NIL, Erlang, Newsqueak, Napier, Hermes, Sather, Alef, and Limbo.
Hoare described the language as 'technology from the past come to save the future from itself.'

A.answer: Graydon Hoare created Rust in 2006 as a personal project while working at Mozilla. The language first appeared publicly on January 20, 2012, with Rust 0.1 released for Windows, Linux, and macOS.

B.answer: Graydon Hoare created Rust in 2006 while working at Mozilla. "The first appeared" date was January 19, 2012, when Rust 0.1 became the first public release.

rows.ask: What is this discussion about, and what is the main disagreement?

core: BrandonM criticizes an app for not offering functionality that Linux users can already build themselves using FTP, curlftpfs, SVN, or CVS.
BrandonM argues the app does not replace a USB drive because it fails to solve connectivity problems that USB drives handle.
BrandonM questions the app's business viability, noting it lacks a revenue model without charging users.
dhouston (app creator) responds that users want plug-and-play simplicity, not DIY solutions.
dhouston explains the app uses local folder sync in the background, which differs from online drive approaches that cause UI latency and performance issues on Windows.
dhouston clarifies the use case is offline access on planes, where Dropbox syncs when reconnected without manual copying.
dhouston reveals the business model is freemium: free tier with a GB limit, then tiered paid plans.

The main disagreement is whether the app solves a real problem: BrandonM sees it as unnecessary duplication, while dhouston frames it as superior user experience for practical scenarios like plane travel.
adjacent: BrandonM notes most people email files or host them online but still carry USB drives as backup.
dhouston points out Windows online drive implementations (CIFS, WebDAV) hide latency poorly and break when applications expect local disk performance.
dhouston references Joel Spolsky's article on leaky abstractions to explain why remote storage feels slow in practice.
dhouston illustrates the performance problem: saving a 20MB file with a 40KB/sec upstream connection would stall the system for 8 minutes.
dhouston contrasts document work on online drives to 'walking around with cinder blocks tied to your feet.'
dhouston describes the specific offline use case: accessing most recent document versions on a plane without network.
BrandonM acknowledges the app works well for Windows users and that background sync is a good design point.
BrandonM notes he experienced minor lagging with curlftpfs in Linux.
BrandonM concedes that claiming the app replaces USB drives is a 'bad idea in general,' suggesting the app's marketing claim is overstated.
The discussion is framed as pre-launch feedback on what appears to be Dropbox before public release.
dhouston mentions unannounced features that have viral potential.
BrandonM expresses hope the feedback helps dhouston anticipate future criticisms.
Both participants agree efficient background sync is technically valuable.

A.answer: This is an early Dropbox pitch thread (2008). BrandonM critiques the service on three fronts: (1) Linux users can already build equivalent systems with FTP+curlftpfs+SVN/CVS; (2) it doesn't truly replace USB drives since it requires connectivity, whereas USB handles offline scenarios; (3) the business model is unclear—without direct charges, revenue viability is uncertain. dhouston (Dropbox founder) counters that plug-and-play matters more than DIY feasibility, that Dropbox solves Windows latency/UX problems via local sync (unlike slow network mounts), handles airplane/offline access via cached files, and will monetize via freemium tiers. BrandonM concedes the Windows UX case is strong but maintains the 'USB replacement' claim is overreaching; dhouston clarifies Dropbox targets the specific use-case of accessing recent files offline, not all USB scenarios.

B.answer: This is an early Dropbox pitch thread on Hacker News. BrandonM critiques the service on three grounds: (1) Linux users can already build similar systems with FTP + curlftpfs + SVN/CVS; (2) it doesn't truly replace USB drives because it fails offline; (3) the business model is unclear. The creator (dhouston) counters that plug-and-play UX matters more than DIY alternatives, that Dropbox solves latency/sync problems Windows file systems create (e.g., CIFS/WebDAV lock-up on remote access), and that it handles offline sync—syncing "everything up when you get back online." He also hints at an unannounced freemium model. The core disagreement is whether Dropbox is genuinely novel given existing tools, and whether it solves real pain points or just repackages them.

rows.ask: What is ruff and what are its main features?

core: Ruff is an extremely fast Python linter and code formatter written in Rust.
Ruff is 10-100x faster than existing linters like Flake8 and formatters like Black.
Ruff supports over 900 built-in lint rules with native re-implementations of popular Flake8 plugins.
Ruff provides drop-in parity with Flake8, isort, and Black.
Ruff can replace Flake8, Black, isort, pydocstyle, pyupgrade, and autoflake while executing tens or hundreds of times faster.
Ruff is installable via pip and can be invoked with uvx, uv, pip, or pipx.
Ruff provides fix support for automatic error correction such as removing unused imports.
Ruff includes built-in caching to avoid re-analyzing unchanged files.
adjacent: Ruff is backed by Astral, the creators of uv and ty.
The GitHub repository has 48,996 stars and 2,302 forks.
Ruff is written in Rust and released under the MIT License.
Ruff supports Python 3.14 compatibility.
Ruff is configured through pyproject.toml, ruff.toml, or .ruff.toml files.
Ruff has first-party editor integrations for VS Code and other editors.
Ruff is monorepo-friendly with hierarchical and cascading configuration.
Ruff is used by major open-source projects including Apache Airflow, FastAPI, Hugging Face, Pandas, and SciPy.
Ruff re-implements over 60 Flake8 plugins and related tools such as flake8-bugbear, eradicate, and tryceratops.
Ruff provides a playground at play.ruff.rs for testing.
Ruff can be used as a pre-commit hook, VS Code extension, and GitHub Action.
Ruff enables F, E, B, UP, and RUF rule categories by default, omitting stylistic rules that overlap with formatters.
Ruff's formatter is built on a fork of Rome's rome_formatter and draws from Rome, Prettier, and Black.
Ruff's import resolver is based on Pyright's import resolution algorithm.
The default line length is 88 characters, matching Black.
Ruff uses double quotes for strings by default, matching Black's behavior.
Ruff is used by companies including Anthropic, Amazon, Databricks, Microsoft, and Netflix.
Ruff's linter draws on APIs and implementation details from Flake8, Pyflakes, pycodestyle, pydocstyle, pyupgrade, and isort.
